stageInfo.what: Lab discovery, then three rounds of human trials: first for safety, then for the right dose, then large efficacy trials across several countries. The trials alone usually take 3 to 6 years.
stageInfo.who: The manufacturer, often with a product development partnership such as MMV
stageInfo.stall: Recruiting enough patients, and running trial sites in several countries.

stageInfo.what: A stringent regulator reviews the full evidence on quality, safety and effectiveness. For malaria medicines this is usually the European Medicines Agency (EMA) EU-M4all procedure (formerly Article 58), which covers medicines meant for use outside Europe. Every later step builds on this opinion. Health authority review status is generally not public, so this step changes only when a regulator or the manufacturer announces an outcome.
stageInfo.who: EMA, or another stringent regulator such as the US FDA
stageInfo.stall: Preparing the full dossier, then waiting out the review.

stageInfo.what: A WHO expert group weighs clinical evidence and decides whether the medicine is included in WHO guidelines for malaria.
stageInfo.who: WHO Department of Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases (MNT) and its Guidelines Development Group
stageInfo.stall: The group meets on its own calendar, so the timing is hard to predict.

stageInfo.what: A separate WHO check of quality and manufacturing, including factory inspections. Prequalification supports eligibility for purchase under the quality assurance and procurement policies of UN agencies and major funders such as the Global Fund; specific policies and exceptions may differ. Manufacturers are invited to apply through a WHO Expression of Interest (EOI).
stageInfo.stall: Waiting for an invitation round, then for inspections.

stageInfo.what: Each country's own regulator licenses the medicine before it can be sold or used there, usually one country at a time. Regional routes, such as the African Medicines Agency and WHO's collaborative registration (about 90 working days), are intended to speed this up.
stageInfo.stall: Going country by country, each with its own queue.

stageInfo.what: Ministries of Health include the medicine in national treatment guidelines. These decide what health workers prescribe and what the public sector buys.
stageInfo.who: Ministries of Health and national malaria programmes
stageInfo.stall: National guideline committees meet rarely and follow their own schedules.

stageInfo.what: Public funders, such as the Global Fund, other donors and national governments, run tenders, agree reference prices and forecast demand. A medicine can be recommended, registered and in the guidelines and still be barely bought. This step covers public channels only: the figures shown are Global Fund-financed procurement. Private commercial channels are not included.
stageInfo.who: The Global Fund, other donors, UNICEF and national governments
stageInfo.stall: Financing cycles. Global Fund grants, for example, run for three years.
stageInfo.source: Global Fund price and quality reporting

stageInfo.what: Supply from port to health facility, health-worker training, and pharmacovigilance once the medicine is in use.
stageInfo.stall: Supply chain readiness and health-worker training.

glossary.ACT: Artemisinin-based combination therapy — the standard class of malaria treatments pairing an artemisinin derivative with a longer-acting partner drug.
glossary.SRA: Stringent Regulatory Authority — the older WHO term for an advanced regulator such as EMA or the US FDA. WHO is replacing it with WHO-Listed Authorities (WLA), regulators assessed against WHO's performance indicators; existing SRAs are treated as WHO-listed during the transition.
glossary.WLA: WHO-Listed Authority — a regulator assessed by WHO as operating at an advanced level.
glossary.EU-M4all: EU-Medicines for all, formerly the Article 58 procedure — EMA's scientific opinion on high-priority medicines intended for markets outside the EU.
glossary.GDG: Guidelines Development Group — the WHO expert group that reviews evidence and formulates treatment recommendations.
glossary.PQ: WHO prequalification — the quality, safety and efficacy assessment whose outcome, a listing on the WHO prequalified-products list, supports eligibility under the quality assurance (QA) and procurement policies of UN agencies and major funders; specific policies and exceptions may differ.
glossary.MFT: Multiple first-line therapies — the deliberate, managed use of two or more effective ACTs in a population for treatment of uncomplicated malaria, either simultaneously or in rotation.
glossary.EOI: Expression of Interest — the WHO prequalification invitation list; a product must be on it before a PQ dossier can be assessed.
glossary.AMA: African Medicines Agency — the African Union's continental medicines agency, based in Kigali, set up to harmonise regulation across the member states that have ratified its treaty and to evaluate selected priority products. National regulators still grant marketing authorisation.
glossary.PMI: U.S. President's Malaria Initiative — a major bilateral funder and procurer of malaria commodities.
glossary.MMV: Medicines for Malaria Venture — product development partnership behind several antimalarials.
glossary.PQR: Price & Quality Reporting — the Global Fund database of procurement transactions (volumes and prices).
glossary.GMP: Good Manufacturing Practice — quality standard verified by inspection of manufacturing sites.

changelog.plain: We checked every claim on the medicine pages against its source. Claims that no published result supports were removed or reworded, and some statements were corrected: most DHA–PPQ presentations rely on a single supplier of the main ingredient, ASPY's 2025 pregnancy label covers the second and third trimesters, and the ALAQ development partnership is now named correctly.
The regulatory approval step now reads "Not started": a submission is being prepared, but none has been announced. We also removed some claims that were not attributed to a source.

We updated several definitions in the glossary, including multiple first-line therapies (MFT) and WHO prequalification, to match current WHO and EMA terminology. Procurement is now shown as transactions and value, with packs listed by presentation and treatment courses only where they can be counted; the figures cover Global Fund-recorded purchases only.

The medicines table now shows two milestones instead of one open-ended count: the year a medicine reached market access (recommended and prequalified by WHO), and how long it has been moving towards access in countries since then. We also explain what "Delayed" means, and a new About LAUNCH section explains why the dashboard follows these four medicines.

Each stage and milestone now links to the public source behind it, and we added 14 references to the Sources list. We removed ALAQ's target dates for approval and WHO prequalification, which no public source confirms, and corrected a few details to match the sources. No statuses changed.

We updated the name of WHO's malaria department to the Department of Malaria and Neglected Tropical Diseases (MNT). The country counts for ASPY and DHA–PPQ now match the country access map, and we show how many countries a national medicines register confirms. We removed the years-late figures until the way they are worked out is agreed; the expected time for each stage stays. ALAQ's description now says it is still in clinical development and that its future role depends on trial results, regulators, WHO and countries. ASPY's description now says that registration and adoption vary by country and that LAUNCH is checking them country by country. For DHA–PPQ we explain what the 0.9–4.5% is a share of, describe its uses more carefully, and corrected Nigeria's count of active registrations from 26 to 25. No dates or statuses changed.

We reworded the explanations of the steps on the pathway after partner feedback, and renamed the first two steps "R&D and Clinical" and "Stringent Regulatory Approval (SRA)". No dates, statuses or figures changed.

Each approved medicine now shows how many years late it is against the time each step is expected to take, with a new Time taken table. The expected times are LAUNCH's working estimates, except country registration, and are still to be agreed.

The country access map now shows only countries we can back with an official or peer-reviewed source. Some countries moved stage, some were added, and those we could not confirm now show No data. New sources include four national medicine registers and WHO's guide to using several first-line treatments. The country counts in each medicine's details now match the map.

We changed some wording after reviewer feedback. The price card is gone, the procurement step is labelled as public channels only, and the page now says that health-authority review progress is usually not public. GanLum now credits Novartis as its developer, with the required acknowledgement of its funders, and the page has a disclaimer.

We removed the drug-resistance results from the map. For that information, the page now points to the WHO Malaria Threats Map. The map's filters and legend have been tidied up, and you can now click any country to see its page.
We now call a blocked step an "access barrier" instead of a "bottleneck". Only the wording changed — no figures or dates were altered.

We found a real example of a country acting on the World Health Organization's advice: Ghana added this medicine as a backup first-choice treatment in 2022. It's still the only country confirmed to have done so. We also recorded the years Global Fund purchasing began for both underused medicines (2018 and 2008).
Everything we checked during the August review is now part of the main dataset. The separate preview version has been retired.

We checked Nigeria's and Tanzania's official medicine registers. Tanzania lists 10 approved versions of this medicine, all up to date. Nigeria lists 47, but only 26 are still active — 22 have expired and would need renewing.
We checked the official medicine registers: Tanzania approved this medicine in 2022, and Nigeria approved a version for children in February 2024. Both are now confirmed on the map.
We corrected the year the World Health Organization first recommended this medicine. It was 2010, not 2015.
We updated the name of the main trial and reworded how we describe the medicine, so both match what the published sources actually say.
We reworded how we describe this medicine to match the manufacturer's own words: the first major change in malaria treatment in more than 25 years.
First batch of updates drawn from public databases — Global Fund purchasing records, World Health Organization approval lists, European medicines records and clinical trial registries.

Purchasing figures added: the Global Fund has bought 11.5 million packs (US$41.5m) since 2008, with a sharp rise in 2025. Nine versions of the medicine have passed World Health Organization quality checks.
Purchasing figures added: the Global Fund has bought 940,000 packs (US$14.5m) since 2018, most of it in 2025 for Uganda and Burkina Faso. The European medicines decision date is now recorded.
The main trial finished on 25 November 2025 with 1,720 participants — now confirmed from the public trial registry.
Added a poster view showing where each medicine sits in development.
Added a country map, a chart of how long each step takes, a shareable widget, an updates feed and automatic snapshots of the data.
Renamed from Pyramax to ASPY. The brand name still appears underneath.
Added plain-language definitions, a download button, a print view, and the time taken between steps.
The main trial succeeded, announced on 12 November 2025. Work on the application for approval has now begun.
Corrected a European approval date to 2012, and added the July 2025 update to the medicine's label for use in pregnancy.
Recorded that Eurartesim passed its World Health Organization quality re-check in January 2025. Figures we cannot yet confirm are shown as TBC.
The dashboard moved from placeholder examples to real information gathered from public sources. Prices and volumes show as TBC until they are confirmed.
